---
title: Connect an app with OAuth
sidebar_label: Connect an app with OAuth
description: Register an app or a web page, get the owner's approval by the code flow or the device flow, and keep its access token fresh.
job: A builder signs an app or a web page in with the owner's approval, by the code flow or the device flow, and keeps its token fresh.
---

An app connects with **OAuth**: the owner approves it once in their browser, and the app receives an access token that begins `marfa_at_`. It goes in the same `Authorization` header as a key and reaches only what the owner approved. **No app ever needs the owner's password.** A script uses a [key](/use/manage-keys) instead, sent as [a request shows](/reference/api#send-a-request).

The instance is its own authorization server. Its discovery document at `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` names the endpoints under `/oauth/`, and **every client is public**: it holds no secret and proves itself with PKCE. In Swift, `Authorization` takes every step, as [the Swift SDK](/reference/swift-sdk/server-calls#sign-in) shows. An MCP client follows them by itself.

## Register the app

Registration needs no credential. A scope is a type and a level, such as `core.file.image:read`, a [permission](/build/access#what-a-credential-reaches), or `offline_access` for a refresh token:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_name": "Photo frame",
  "application_type": "native",
  "redirect_uris": ["com.example.frame:/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "scope": "core.file.image:read offline_access"
}
```

Marfa answers `201` with the `client_id`. **Name the scopes the app needs:** a registration with none gets the [default scopes](/catalog/permissions), read and write on all content and its edges.

The redirect address decides the kind. A **web** client, the default, takes `https` addresses off the loopback. A **native** client may also use `http://127.0.0.1` with any port, or a reverse domain name you control as a scheme, as above. An app can instead name itself by the `https` address of a client ID metadata document, as [Register an OAuth client](/reference/api/apps/registerOAuthClient) shows.

## Send the owner to approve

Make a random verifier and keep it. Its challenge is the base64url SHA-256 of it, and Marfa takes only `S256`. Open the authorization endpoint in the owner's browser with the challenge and a `state` of your own:

```http title="Request"
GET /oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=<client_id>&redirect_uri=com.example.frame%3A%2Fcallback&scope=core.file.image%3Aread%20offline_access&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&state=<state>
```

The owner signs in if needed and approves the app, as [Connect your agent](/connect-your-agent#approve-what-it-may-reach) shows. A write or a permission needs a sign-in from the last fifteen minutes, so the page may ask the owner to confirm it's them. Marfa then sends the browser to your redirect address with `code`, `state` and `iss`. Check that **`state` is the one you sent** and `iss` is the instance's issuer. A denial carries `error=access_denied` and no code.

## Exchange the code for tokens

Post the code and the verifier to `/oauth/token` as a form:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=<code>&redirect_uri=com.example.frame%3A%2Fcallback&client_id=<client_id>&code_verifier=<verifier>
```

Marfa answers `200` with an `access_token` that lasts `expires_in` seconds (3600), a `refresh_token` if the app asked for `offline_access`, and `scope`, which **can be less than you asked for**. A code works once: sending it again answers `400 invalid_grant` and ends the tokens it gave.

Before the access token expires, post `grant_type=refresh_token`, the `refresh_token` and the `client_id` to the same endpoint. **Each exchange ends the refresh token you sent**, so store the new one first. A used refresh token answers `400 invalid_grant` and ends every token in its chain, and the app asks the owner again.

To disconnect, post the refresh token to `POST /oauth/revoke`, which ends the app's tokens and the owner's approval. The owner can also cut an app off, as [See and revoke access](/use/see-and-revoke-access) shows. The `/oauth/` endpoints answer errors in OAuth's own shape, not the [error envelope](/reference/errors).

## Connect with the device flow

A command-line tool or a device with no browser shows the owner a short code to approve elsewhere, as `marfa login` does. Register a native client with no redirect address and the grant `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. Then ask for a code, naming the scopes, since a request with none answers `400 invalid_scope`:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/device-authorization
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=<client_id>&scope=core.file%3Aread%20offline_access
```

Marfa answers `user_code`, `verification_uri` and `device_code`. Show the owner the first two, then post `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` with the `device_code` and `client_id` to `/oauth/token`, **waiting `interval` seconds between requests**. Until the owner decides, Marfa answers `400 authorization_pending`, or `400 slow_down` when you ask too soon. Approval gives the same tokens as the code exchange.

## Connect a web page

A web page takes the same steps in its own script, registered as a web client, with no setup on the instance and no key. It needs an `https` address with a real host name, so a page on `http://localhost` can't connect, and a callback page at its redirect address. Open the approval in a small window from a click, listen first for the callback, and keep only the answer that carries your `state`:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const answered = new Promise<URLSearchParams>((resolve) => {
  const channel = new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval");
  channel.onmessage = (event) => {
    const answer = new URLSearchParams(event.data);
    if (answer.get("state") !== state) return;
    channel.close();
    resolve(answer);
  };
});
open(authorizeUrl, "marfa-approval", "popup,width=480,height=640");
```

The callback page runs at the page's own origin, so it passes the result over the channel and closes:

```html title="callback.html"
<script>
  new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval").postMessage(location.search);
  close();
</script>
```

The page then exchanges the code as above, with `fetch`. **Don't send `credentials: "include"`:** Marfa allows no credentials on a cross-origin answer, so the access token is the page's only authority. An owner who closes the window sends nothing, so let the page cancel the wait. For a browser that blocks windows, redirect the whole page instead and keep the verifier and `state` in `sessionStorage`.

Approving the page lets the origin of each redirect address it registered call the instance from a browser, until the last app approved there is disconnected. An owner can name an origin in advance with the `cors_origins` [setting](/run/settings). A registration nobody approves is removed after an hour idle, so register again until the owner approves, then keep the `client_id`.

The rules are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md#web-pages) chapter of the contract.
